name: Antarctic shilajit

lead: Antarctic shilajit appears as an entry among 'mumioids', natural substances resembling shilajit, the tar-like humic material from mountain rock crevices used in Ayurvedic and other traditional medicine. Beyond that listing, little is documented about it.

Shilajit itself is sold as a supplement for vitality, and a 2024 systematic review reported that one purified extract may increase testosterone in men with late-onset hypogonadism. That research concerns shilajit generally rather than the Antarctic material.

paras: Shilajit-type products are typically sold as resin, powder or capsules. No documented practice specific to Antarctic shilajit is available.
Some shilajit sources have been found in studies to contain hazardous heavy metals including lead. Nothing is documented on the safety of Antarctic material specifically.

angle.text: Shilajit-type substances are taken in the belief they support energy and testosterone, which users connect to training and body composition. For the Antarctic variety specifically, no practice or results are documented.

lead: Antarctic shilajit is named in encyclopedic lists of mumioids, a group of substances that resemble shilajit, which also includes ozokerite, saltpeter and fossilised resins [1]. Shilajit is a thick, sticky, blackish-brown exudate from mountain rock crevices in regions such as the Himalayas, Altai and Caucasus, composed largely of humic substances (about 60 to 80 percent) with minerals and organic compounds [1].

People take shilajit for energy, vitality and testosterone support, which they tie to training capacity and body composition. Wikipedia reports a 2011 review finding limited evidence of benefit in traditional Indian medicine and a 2024 systematic review tentatively reporting a testosterone increase with a purified extract in men with late-onset hypogonadism [1]. These findings concern shilajit, not Antarctic material, and no studies on Antarctic shilajit itself are known.

paras: Wikipedia's shilajit article places Antarctic shilajit in a list of mumioids and gives no further description [1]. Shilajit proper is described as an organic-mineral product of predominantly biological origin, with proposed origins in microbial breakdown of oil-bearing rock, decayed resinous plants or mosses [1].

Shilajit has been used in folk medicine for thousands of years, including in Ayurveda, Chinese and Tibetan medicine [1]. A 2011 review found limited evidence of benefit, and a 2024 systematic review reported a possible testosterone increase with a purified extract; the same article notes studies finding hazardous heavy metals, including lead, in some sources [1].
No studies found. Research on shilajit generally is summarised above and does not address the Antarctic material.
